title: Tom Albert and Milton "Mooney" Martin Interview, 1964-12-21

blocks.x: This is Bill Russell speaking. We're interviewing Mr. Milton Martin. Is that your full name? Over at Tom Albert's house on Burgundy Street, where we used to interview Mr. Albert and Vess and other people were here the last time I was here. Can you give us your full name? Everybody calls you Mooney.
Milton Martin.
Milton Martin. How did you get that name of Mooney?
Well, that's a nickname.
Just a nickname. That's a nickname. Can you tell us when you were born, if you don't mind, about how old you are?
Born in 1896.
1896. That's right. And what was the exact date?
24th of November.
24th of November. Where was that? On this side of the river or the other side?
On the other side, Algiers.
About what part of Algiers?
Algiers, low coast.
Down, as they call it, down the low coast there. That's right. That was past the naval station.
Right past the naval station.
Is it as far as the cutoff? There's a place I never did know just where the cutoff is.
Right where George Lewis lives.
About where George Lewis lives now, down in that section. Down in that section. Did your parents play any musical instruments?
I had an uncle, Amos, he played music. That was before I was born. Yes. What instrument did he play? He played bass horn. Bass. Amos Martin.
Yeah.
He got drowned.
Do you remember what band he played with? Did you hear what bands he played with?
No, I never did know the band. That was before I was born.
Before you were born.
See, he was born in slavery, Amos.
Yep.
That's the slavery time.
And your father didn't play anything then? No. Or your mother, did she play any instrument or sing? I guess she would sing probably.
I had a... Of course, you went to his house. We called him Shamrock. His name was George Stewart.
George Stewart.
Yeah.
And they called him Shamrock.
Yeah. I didn't know that. Yeah, you know the... Remember when we went over to his house? Me, you, slow-dragging... Wait a minute. George Lewis.
I don't remember. No, I can't remember that. When was that? How long? Long ago? That's around the 40s. That far back.
I guess I just forgot about that. When he played the piano in his wife's song, son's song.
Oh, yeah. Where did they live?
Where was... They lived over in a place called Oakdale on Farragore Street.
Oakdale.
Yeah. Yeah. Two years over there.
Yeah, that's right. I forgot about that. See, those days you were living over here on...
Oh, I've been living over here since... Dolphin, though. I've been living over here since around 19... 6. 19-6.
That far back.
Yeah, that far back. Yep.
The other night, we were over at Preservation Hall and Peter Bokhauser's playing, and you mentioned about the first time you ever heard him.
Can you tell us? 1905. 1905. 1905. 1905 with Tom Albert at the Flying Mexican Hall.
The Flying Mexican Hall.
That's right. That's the Flying Mexican Hall. Down in Jules's Lane. Was that Algiers? That's Algiers. Over in Algiers. Jules's Lane.
About where is that? Down...
That's one block where you get off the bus to George Lewis, one block that way to George Lewis House.
Down towards...
In that same section? In that same section.
And there was a hall down there?
Yeah, Flying Mexican Hall. Mm-hmm.
What was the hall like? Was it fairly big or a little one there?
Well, it was a pretty good-sized hall.
Made out of wood, not brick or anything?
Made out of wood. It was a wood hall.
Wood hall. Who ran it, and what went on there? Dances. It had dances. Dances. Dances. Usually on weekends or what night?
On weekends. On Saturday nights.
Saturday. Did they have a manager for the hall or anything?
The manager, the owner of the hall was James McGee. James McGee. I remember you told me the other night. James McGee. But we used to call him Jimmy McGee.
Jimmy McGee.
But his name was James McGee.
And he was over across the river too, lived over there, didn't he?
Right there. That's the place that, the lots and the house there now, one of the houses.
Oh, it is. It's still there.
Yeah.
I know there's a little church over there on that street where George lives. The artist.
That's right around the corner.
Right around the corner.
Where you get to that street where George's at. Yeah. Right around the corner.
And they had dances there.

Oh, yeah. That way. That way. He had Peter. Fess. And. And. And. And. And. And. Uh. Nutzer Rubin. Who was that? Nutzer Rubin. What did he play? He played banjo. Guitar. Guitar. Yeah. They got guitar. They got guitar. Eddie Vinson playing trombone. And he was playing trumpet. Yeah. What did Peter play those days? Peter. Yeah. Peter was playing violin and trumpet like him. Yeah. That was around 1905 because I little fella peeping through the hole my mama and them was in there dancing and I'm peeping through the hole.
See, you were born in 96. Yes right. You were only about nine or ten years old, hardly ten years old. That's right.

That's right. And along that time, you take, Luriat was running, that's what the white place up there at the naval station, they were playing there. They had bands up there, you played there too Tom? Yeah, I played there. Yeah, Peter and Peter. But now before you had Peter and then you had my father-in-law there, Edmund Payton. Edmund Payton. Edmund Payton. So what did Payton play? He played bass and banjo, guitar.
Seems like I once heard something about Payton had an accordion band or something. Did he ever play accordion or did he have any?
Yeah, Payton used to play over here. That's on Franklin Street, we called it Franklin Street. That was a different Payton. Yes, a different Payton. Different Payton.

Now, before you timed there, right along, it was old, the band was there in that section. That was old man. Dorsey? No, no, Dorsey was up further. They take Ruben Manuel and them was down in there. Ruben Manuel, you remember old man Ruben Manuel?
Yeah, that's why they had the brass band.

Yeah. Ruben Manuel and Harry, he used to play drum in there man. Under that tree. Under that tree. Right down there under that tree. Jill Davis. Jill, but now them people be hundred after they be there.

Sure would. I remember Manuel Mineta showed us a big tree not far from his house over there on Leboeuf Street where they had picnics when he was a boy. Would it be near there? That's full of them. Up near these railroad tracks and all, not far from that.
You're talking about Whitney Avenue, that big old oak tree.
Yeah, it was up there near Whitney.
That big old oak tree. That's that.
This was a different tree you were talking about.

Yeah, yeah, this tree was down in old Harry's Yard. You used to come down there when I was a kid and play. Oh yeah, I played down in Harry's Yard. I was a kid, used to play down there. Yeah. You see, Harry had that black horse and used to set me up on the horse while they all played music.
That's been good a long time.

Oh yeah. I had been back there around 1903, four, or back up in the five. Then around 1907, six and seven, that's when they went to Pickle. On the boat. On the boat. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. See, Saul Morgan and August Schaeber built that, drive them piling down there so the boat could land and the boat used to leave them up there at Canal Street and go down there and have them picnics. Right down there at Pickle. That's the place Nani called Arula Garden. Arula Garden.
Oh yes. That's down below where George lives.
That's right.

And that was for colored people on the boat that you were telling the other night. They had those sort of excursions for colored people on that boat. That's right. That's right. On them boats. And they'd pick up the people on this side at Canal.
Both sides. Both sides. Both sides. They'd get on there and they'd get on and they'd have the picnics and things.

And they called that place Pickles? Pickles. Pickles. Pickles. What was the name of the boat do you remember? The Bell of the Bend. The Bell of the Bend. Was it a pretty big boat or what did it look like?
Yeah, yeah. Big boats. Yeah. Big boats. Yeah.
Big boats. Bell of the Bend. Then they had a, did they have a band play on the boat too?
Oh yeah. All them bands and called them different bands. Yeah. Used them all the same. Yeah.
I thought maybe they just took them down to the picnic and then had the band there at the

picnic. No. They were on the boat cause I never remember when they used to swing out. I had written. Yeah. Running from Connell Street Ferry down there. Oh yeah. See when they used to swing out from Connell Street there, the team song was Ho Alley's Ho. Never forget my partner, never do my partner what you did to me. Ho Alley's Ho. I never get better. Did I play on that?
Huh? I played a little job on that. Yeah, you played on that.
Yeah, I went on the Pickles too. Sure.
I played down there on that, but we played on the gallery. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. That big hall.
Big gallery. Big gallery.
Yeah.
And they built a special wharf for the boat to land on. For the boat to land. Then they started the hall there where they played in the hall or was it outdoors?
No, it was a lawn opening. Like a lawn. Two rows of trees with a lawn in between them two rows of trees. Well that's where the picnic.
Yeah. Did they have a fence around it so other people couldn't get in?
Yeah, they had a fence. Yeah, the fence. Of course the people that went on the boat, well they went on in. Yeah, they went on in there.
I just wondered other people around there.
They didn't go on the boat, well they had to pay to come in.
They had to come in then. Yeah. Can you remember any of the other bands that played there? Different ones?
No, I don't remember the other bands because I was small. Yeah, it was pretty small. Pretty small.
You could hear them all the way down though, from the river. You could hear them as they went along.

Oh yeah. I was following it. Yeah. I was on the levee. Run down the levee. Run down the levee, follow it from Cunhal Street down there. You could hear it all the way. All the way down. Follow that. Wish I could have heard that. Now you take, after that you take, had a fella down there they called Joe Yetta. Joe? Joe Yetta. He run the ballroom, they had a hole down there at the Cut-Off. Yeah. When I, he used to play down there.
Tommy played there?

Yeah, I played down there. That's right. Played down there. And then. What year that was in? Oh, that's, that's around 1907, the eight. Back up in there. Yeah. Because Charlie McDonough, he was, he come there after Julietta. Yeah. Charlie McDonough, the colored fella. They all played there for Charlie McDonough. Yeah, I played for all of them. He was the manager then, the Dungle of the Spikes. That's right, Charlie McDonough.

You mentioned a few minutes ago about Vinson, the trombone, Eddie Vinson, the trombone player. I never did get to see him or hear him. He died so long ago, I guess up in Chicago. Yeah, he died. Can you tell us any more about him, what he was like and anything, do you know anything about his family or folks, where he came from?
Yeah, I know his family. He came out of John's source, he raised up with him. Yeah, yeah. I married his cousin. You married his cousin?

Yeah, I married his cousin and we, we played together and his father, we was learning together, me and him. So he was playing routine and I learned him the music. Yeah. I learned him the music. He was playing routine and I learned him the music and so him and Nussie Rubin was playing, had a professor over here from the French opera. Where did you see that? No, right here. You know the French opera they had, yeah. Yeah, Rubin and Toulouse. Yeah, well he used to come over here and take lessons, Nussie Rubin, with his trombone. So Eddie used to come over with him and so the professor told him, he said don't bring that fellow over here no more. Because Nussie was paying, paying for the lesson and Eddie was testing it all. He was doing most of the lesson. Yeah. So Eddie took up the horn and he went, come on and made a couple of notes on the horn. He told him don't bring that fellow over here no more. He's a French fellow, right in the French quarters here. Yeah. So we learned together. We wear the same clothes. Yeah. He was a dad and I married his sister in the house, in his house. And where did he live about in Algeria? He lived in a place called Socks' Lane. John Socks' Lane.
Right behind the Naval Station. Right behind the Naval Station.
Yeah, that's what we learned right there. And me and him was together. We learned together, we played together for years. You say his father played something too or not?
No, his father was a caulker. His father was a caulker. Didn't play any? No, no, at all.
No.
And we uh. Did he have any brothers or anybody else in the family that played music? No. Just Eddie.
No, just Eddie. Cause his sister, none of them didn't play no music. Just Eddie. We didn't just stay there and played on the ground. And we had a band.

learn together. So I took my lesson at a place they called Jimmy, Jimmy, we called him Jimmy Spree. Yeah, yeah. That's right. His grandmother was it that raised him? His grandmother raised him. That's the name that. You know what they call him? Verrett and Homer. I used to go there twice a week. And Jimmy taught you then on violin? Did he teach you anything on cornet too? No, no. Just the violin? No. So the violin got too slow for me. So I picked up the cornet myself. I know the music. All I wanted are the scales. So I think nobody that showed me doesn't know the cornet. So I bought a book, an ABC book, and I learned the scales and I always went through myself. I never took a little less no no cornet. No no trumpet. So I just learned being edited together.
The violin got too slow. Yeah, and Eddie, that was always his main instrument, trombone I guess. Did he play anything else? Yeah, yeah. He played saxophone.
Oh, he played saxophone. He came here in 1918 when Sam Langford and Georgie Nett

된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된 then did he go with any other band that you remember?
Yeah, yeah he went with the George Barca and then the Olympia. The Olympia. Yeah, the Olympia.
Freddie Kepler.
Freddie Kepler and then. Yeah. Freddie Kepler. Freddie Kepler. Freddie, him Freddie. And Bill Johnson was with him for a while I know.
Yeah, Bill Johnson. And Jimmy Puller. That's right. And George Barca.
Yeah. Not him the one left here.
I met a guitar player out in Los Angeles, oh twenty years or more ago, twenty-five years ago. And they called him Giggy Williams. His real name is Norwood Williams.
He played guitar.

Norwood Williams. He was with that band out on the road. I don't know if he played with them here, but he came from, do you remember him, a guitar player? Did he? No, Giggy. G-I-G-I is the way I spelled it. Giggy. Giggy Williams. Norwood Williams was his real name. Williams.
I don't remember.
I guess he left here so long ago that most people didn't remember him here.

When he left here in 16, Billy Moran was playing drum, playing bass with him. Billy Moran, yeah. That's right. Billy Moran was playing bass with that bunch. With that bunch, but they left. Yeah. But Billy Moran didn't leave. He stayed here. He stayed here. You know, let's see, Bebe was beating drum for me. Bebe Matthews? That's right. Oh, yeah. Bebe was beating drums. What was his last name? That's his name, Bebe Matthews. Oh, Matthews.
Oh, I didn't get, yeah.
But they was calling him Tyke. His nickname, they called him Tyke.
Yeah, I never knew him. I knew Bill Matthews as the only brother I knew.
Well, they had four of them, and all of them was drummers.
And one of them worked on the boat, and I didn't even know it. That was Remus. Remus, yeah. I guess I saw him a lot of times, didn't even know it.
And he was a good drummer, too.
Yeah, I wish I'd talk to him. He didn't play those last years, I guess.
No, he stopped. The last time he played was in the Island Band.
Oh, about Eddie Vinson again, did he play a slide trombone always, or did he play the valve sometimes? He played slide. Always the slide.

You see, in 1908, he was playing with Pacific, him and Buddy. Buddy Johnson? Buddy Johnson, yeah. Buddy Johnson, yeah. See, in 1908, that's when he got in that Pacific band. Yeah. He took Frankie Duesen's job in that Pacific band. Eddie Vinson.
You know, what was that Pacific band? Was it the fellows that worked for the railroad or something there? No, no.
Or just called it that? I didn't know if it was. No, no, no.
Just called it that. Just called it that. Because it was that Texas and Pacific railroad, I thought maybe they had a band or something.

No, they meant that band. That was Nomm in them. Nomm, yeah. Nomm. Louis La Rooks? Well, there's Louis La Rooks come after. Nomm. Mineta, that's right. That's right. Yeah. Nomm. Louis La Rooks. Not Nomm. Nomm. Not Louis La Rooks. Louis La Rooks. Louis La Rooks. Louis La Rooks. Joey Hooker? One used to cut meat there. Oh, Louis La Rooks. That's Louis La Rooks. No, they're not. Joel Azard. Oh. Joel Azard. Now, George A Hooker. Then Lodal Rooks come in after. After, after George A Hooker. They had old man George Sims playing biotone. George Davis beating drum. Old man Pekins. He was playing trombone. You had Buddy Johnson playing trombone. You had Dude playing drum. What was Dude's name, other name, do you know?
Dude Calvin. Calvin. Calvin.
Calvin, I think.
Calvin.

I was doing that. I was playing Clannett. Clannett, yeah. I was Gibral. I was Gibral. I was playing Clannett. That's right. You had Joe Pye playing alto. That's right. You're all right now. You take, uh, woman George Sims, he got out. That's where, uh, uh, Clay Dash come in there. Clay Dash come in there playing baritone. You take, uh, and Buddy Dash, he come in there playing trombone. I mean, uh, trumpet. They were two brothers. Buddy and Clay. Dash. Was that last name?
I never heard of him.

Clay Dash, yeah. Then, later, the son. When the Pacific was going out then, that's when Bunny Dash started to come in there beating drum. See, that was the son of Clay Dash. Yeah. He died in, uh, in Baton Rouge. He married and went to Baton Rouge.

About how big a band was that altogether? About how many cornets did they use? Yeah, three cornets. Three cornets. Three cornets. How many trombones? Two. Two. And they used alto horns those days. Alto, alto, biotone, clarinet, bass, snare drum. Two drums, yeah. Yeah, two drums, yeah. Um, I remember Manuel Moneta told us something, I believe, about a band the Southern Pacific had, too. Did they have some of the fellows that worked for them? Well, they- Have a band for the Southern Pacific? I didn't know whether- Well, uh- That wasn't any connection then with the Pacific Grass Band or the Texas and Pacific Railroad. No. I thought maybe they named it after the fellows that worked at the railroad or something at first.

No. That band there, that band was up in the 80s. Pacific Band, cause them long, we were Spanish and American War. Yeah, that's right. Back there. Yeah, that's right. See, back there in 1895, all them people was playing-
They'd been playing that long, yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Maybe longer than that. Who was the leader of the Pacific Band? At that, at the time I know- Joel Lizard. Joel Lizard. Joel Lizard. Yeah, Joel Lizard.
Joel Lizard. No, no, no, Joel Lizard.
Joel Lizard. Joel Lizard. Was the leader. But now, he was playing in there, in tough trumpet player, all of them.
I believe somebody said he played the little E flat horn.
Did he know that little E flat?
Yeah, tough trumpet. Yeah, yeah.
Joel, uh, now, Georgia Hooker, it's another man.
Yeah, I've heard of him, yeah. Tough on the trumpet.
See, tough trumpet players.
Harrison Barnes told us about, uh, Mr. Hooker, he'd worked with him when he came to town.
Yeah, well, now, when he come to town, he was a trumpet player. Yeah.
He got off that trombone, got on trombone.
Yeah.
And baritone horn, too, I guess he played.
Yeah, he played, well, pretty much all of them. He used to play biotone, too. He could play biotone. You did, too, Tom.
Yeah, yeah. And the alto.
Yeah.
Yeah, once you learned the fingering, you could play it. Yeah, yeah.
I played with Allen. I played with Allen, and I played, uh, in Allen with, uh, me and, uh, Lewis, Lewis Armstrong, Allen, and Three Cornets. Yeah, well, that's in the 20s.
That's in the 20s.

Yeah. Yeah. When we went over and played the cornerstone lane in the way, uh, uh, Luch's mother's house there. Yeah. In the Jack, Ron Jack, what's the name of that place? That was, uh, wait, no, that was, uh, Craig Church. Craig Church, yeah. Craig Church. In Algiers over there.
In Algiers.
That was the last time I played with Lewis Armstrong. Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
Yeah. And then he went to Chicago, I guess.
Yeah, then he went back.
Right? He played? He hadn't went then. No, he played on the board. He played on the board. You see? Yeah. Lewis, in 15, Lewis was playing Libby and Padilla. Oh, yes, I remember that.
In Short Pants. Him and Freddie.

The three piece there. I remember. Freddie who? Brian Freddie. Oh, Brian Freddie. Yeah, he blew, he blew his hop and hop. Oh, yes, yeah. I met him, yes. He played clarinet a little too, didn't he? Yeah, with Lewis. In that Libby and Padilla.
Yeah. Then, uh, They had the piano in the band there. Yeah, the piano. Well, they had piano in them places then.
But now you take them to the piano. Yeah.
And then, uh,
They had the piano in the band there.
Yeah, the piano. Well, they had piano in them places then.
Yeah. But now you take them to the piano. They had piano in them. Yeah. But now you take the band was playing, uh, in these halls and things. They didn't have piano then. There was no piano. Yeah.
No. But then some of the honky-tonks did have a piano.
Yeah.
And then, see, I had them. Whose place was that? Do you remember? No.
Liberty and Padilla. I don't know who place was that.
Uh, Bunk used to talk about a fellow they called Mustache that ran that place. Some Italian.

Yeah, he did. Now, You take, uh, Louis played, Play, There's fifteen. Then, uh, You take Manuel and them had the coppery, Or had the economy hall. Manuel Perez. That's right. Manuel and them left here. Around in eighteen. Manuel and them left here. Then, Ori, Joe, Oliver. Baby, Dot and them. They took the economy hall. Eddie Vincent come here and got, uh, Joe Oliver. 된된된된된된된 Then Louis, you take, Piro had the boat. Piro and Peter and them had the boat. But still yet they had a contract for the halfway house back there. They turned the job over to Joe Howell. Joe Howell had Ethan Riley, Amos Riley. Amos Riley, yeah. Amos Riley on trumpet but he didn't suit him. Then where they got together and said we'll try Louis, he's a little rough but we'll gentle him down.
Was that for the boat then?
That was for the boat.
Peter had been on the boat then. Peter had been on the boat. They had left the boat. They had left the boat and turned the job over to Joe Howell. Oh, to Joe Howell. That's right.
And that's when Louis went on the boat.

And then Joe Howell come play with the Riker, with us. Yeah, well that's the, yeah. Yeah, he come play with us, he played tuba. He played tuba then. Yeah, played bass. And then, so he stood with us until Wilson, he died, you know. He died twice didn't he, Joe Howell. Yeah.
Joe Howell. Joe Howell. Joe Howell. Joe Howell. Joe Howell. Joe Howell.
He died. Joe Howell died in the 40s. Yeah, it wasn't so awfully long. He died in the 40s. It's been 20 years now. It doesn't seem so long to me.
So he played us a long time. We, whenever we were playing.
And he was a good musician.
He was a good musician. He was a tough drummer.

Yeah. And now you take, back, 1908. Back, all back up in there. You take McCullen and, they had a tough band. McCullen and, Old Man McCullen. McCullen and Poissy's daddy. Brother Humphrey? Yeah, he's together. Willie Humphrey. Yeah, he's together. See?
Oh, I played with them too. I had him played with me too. The old man, the young man, the two brothers. I played with them all.
Their grandfather was Jim Humphrey, wasn't he? He was a teacher, I think. Yeah, that's the old man.
I went to the old fella, old fella, and took one lesson with him with the clan that. And I went back no more.
Well, that's a long time though.

Of course, a lot of them fellas didn't know them fellas back up in there. No, that's right. Like, now Jimmy Noon, now he started down there with Sam Ross and Churro, Sam Bo. Sam Bo, yeah. Used to play trombone there. That's where he started.
Was that down the coast too? Yeah, yeah. That's at the Cut-Off. At the Cut-Off, yeah. Where did Jimmy Noon come from?
That's where he come from. Stanton. Stanton. But now after Stanton sold the plantation out, Jimmy Noon moved across the river. His family moved across the river.
So where was Stanton? On this side?
Stanton on the other side, down below.
Down below. Do you know anything about Jimmy Noon's family? If his folks played anything or anybody else? Any brothers or?
I was just, he didn't know no older than me.

Yeah. Not there. I knew him in Chicago, but I never talked to him very much and never got much about his life. Yeah. I knew he came from here, but I didn't know it was on the other side even. Yes, on the other side. Yeah, on the other side.
But he started Jimmy Noon just a little before me.
Yeah.
Yeah. And I came up with, after that, Jimmy Noon and Frank Ross. Ross. Sam Ross. Sam Ross. Sam Ross. Sam Ross. Yeah. He was one-eyed. One-eyed. What did he play? Trumpet.
Trumpet.
Yeah.

Did Jimmy Noon start on clarinet, do you think, or did he play anything else first? No, he always played clarinet. Always played clarinet. Always played clarinet. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Always played clarinet.

And you take, when I first knew Wooden Joe, he was playing clarinet. Yeah, I remember, I heard him on clarinet too. He played both of them in his late- You heard him on clarinet? Yeah, I made a record of Wooden Joe on clarinet that time. Yeah? He was playing clarinet. He played the blues, you know.

How he, from the understanding I got, how he got off of clarinet on trumpet, and he cut his fingers, cut his fingers, cut his fingers, cut his hand, and he couldn't... He could move the fingers, but he couldn't bend it.
That's right. Fingers like that stuff. Fingers like that stuff how he got off a clarinet on trumpet, somebody cut his hand, cut his fingers, cut his hand, and he couldn't...
